item.title: [World news | The Guardian] ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished
item.description:
English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work

In the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-town France. He described lazy August swims in the Marne River east of Paris. He wrote about age-gap affairs and semi-incestuous flirtations. Schérer gallantly used a nom de plume, Gilbert Cordier, to shield his Catholic family from scandal, but he needn’t have bothered as his concerns were unfounded. The finished novel, Élisabeth, barely made a ripple and quickly slipped out of print. Undeterred, Scherer adopted a second pseudonym – Éric Rohmer – and decided to try his luck as a film-maker instead.

Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on from its author’s death – Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Guilt, grief and strength: Gaza’s ‘sole survivor’ children face life alone
item.description:
Guilt, grief and strength: Gaza’s ‘sole survivor’ children face life alone

Submitted by Huda Skaik on Fri, 08/21/2026 - 13:25
Thousands of children who lost their families in Israeli strikes navigate grief, trauma and adulthood with little support
A Palestinian mourns the death of Al Jazeera journalist Ahmed Wishah, who was killed in an Israeli strike, at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir el-Balah in the central Gaza Strip in 21 June 2026 (Eyad Baba/AFP)
Off

Every morning, 13-year-old Jana al-Motouq wakes up alone.

The Palestinian girl prepares her own breakfast, washes her clothes and gets ready for school.

Not long ago, those small tasks were done by her mother.

“She used to wake us up, make breakfast, brush our hair,” al-Motouq said. “Now I do everything by myself.”

That is because al-Motouq was the sole survivor of her family after an Israeli strike killed them on 17 November 2023 in the Gaza Strip.

The attack on a residential building in Jabalia killed her parents, Ahmed and Heba; her twin sister Saja; and her younger brothers, Hossam, eight, and Mohammed, four.

She is among thousands of children left without parents, siblings or extended family after Israeli bombardment killed more than 73,000 people over two years. 

Most of Gaza’s 2.2 million people have also been displaced repeatedly, stripped of their homes, schools and the routines that once gave their lives structure.

The result is a generation being forced to grow up amid grief, displacement and profound uncertainty.

Another 35 members of al-Motouq’s extended family, including uncles and cousins, were also killed in the strike.

Al-Motouq survived because she had slept at her grandmother’s house across the street that night after falling ill.

When the explosion shook the neighbourhood shortly before dawn, she rushed outside.

“Our house wasn’t there anymore,” she recalled.

“I kept calling for my mum and dad. I sat on the rubble calling them. Nobody answered.”

Survivor guilt 

For days afterwards, al-Motouq returned to the ruins each morning, searching for traces of the family she had lost.

She picked up bloodstained blankets from the debris, hugging and kissing them, before relatives pulled her away from the danger.

“I wished I had been with them,” she told Middle East Eye. “I thought, if I had died with them, maybe I could rest.”

'I thought, if I had died with them, maybe I could rest'

- Jana al-Motouq, Palestinian girl

That guilt is common among people like al-Motouq in Gaza, according to Sereen al-Absi, a psychologist who has worked with survivors like her.

“They always feel that they are guilty: Why did I survive while they are gone? I didn’t protect them,” al-Absi, 29, told MEE.

“Even though logically they know they had nothing to do with what happened, their feelings cannot control the amount of pain they have experienced.”

Al-Motouq now lives with her maternal grandparents in a tent, after displacement destroyed the life she once knew.

Before the war, she and her twin sister were inseparable.

“We wore the same clothes,” she remembered with a faint smile. “If one of us wore something different, we’d get upset.

“She wasn’t just my twin, she was my life partner.”

‘I wasn’t even able to cry’

According to Riad al-Bitar, undersecretary at the Palestinian Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the war has left more than 68,000 children and adults as sole survivors of their families, as well as more than 75,000 orphans who have lost one or both parents.

The scale of the phenomenon is such that medical personnel in Gaza have adopted the acronym WCNSF - “Wounded Child, No Surviving Family” - to describe patients who arrive at hospitals wounded and alone.

Eighteen-year-old Dima Junina, who lives in Gaza City, was one of them. 

An Israeli bombing on 30 October 2023 caused a building next door to collapse onto their house. 

Her father, Ahmed, her mother, Noor, and her three younger brothers - Anas, Baraa and six-year-old Mufeed - were all killed. 

Junina survived because a door shielded her beneath the rubble. For hours, she believed the rest of her family were still alive.

'I don’t want people treating me differently because I’m an orphan'

- Dima Junina, Palestinian girl

Doctors treated a wound to her head as she begged rescuers for news.

“I kept saying, ‘Please bring my parents and my brothers out.’”

Only at dawn did relatives tell her they had all been killed.

“I wasn’t even able to cry,” she said. “It still feels like they’re going to walk through the door.”

Unlike many people around her, Junina rarely describes herself as a sole survivor. She dislikes being pitied.

“I don’t want people treating me differently because I’m an orphan.”

Sympathy can also bring painful reminders. Classmates sometimes mention her mother without thinking. Teachers occasionally ask students to bring a parent to school.

One English teacher, despite knowing her circumstances, told her to return with her mother after she missed class because she was ill.

“He remembered halfway through the sentence,” she said.

She never returned to his classroom.

Instead, she found teachers who quietly made space for her grief without turning it into a spectacle.

Strength and grief

Both teenagers are now being forced to learn to carry responsibilities their parents once shouldered.

Al-Motouq talks about making tea before school, studying alone, and trying to remain strong because her parents always encouraged her education.

Junina describes becoming “five people in one” - taking on everything her father once handled and everything her mother once managed.

For Gaza's orphans, the safety of childhood vanished with their parents
Bahzad al Akhras
Read More »

“The war made my personality stronger,” she said. “It had to.” 

But strength does not erase grief.

Al-Motouq still accidentally calls classmates by her twin sister’s name. Sometimes she reaches for a pencil expecting Saja to hand it to her.

The trauma she and Junina experience can cause them to withdraw from others or become intensely attached to people who remind them of those they have lost, according to al-Absi.

“It doesn’t necessarily have to be their face; it could be a feeling. So they become attached to that person,” she explained.

The opposite can also happen.

“It can also cause isolation, where you want to isolate yourself.”

Al-Absi said the trauma is compounded because sole survivors carry the grief of every person they have lost.

“It’s caused by losing one, two, three or more people, and it can create a complex form of trauma,” she said.

Wishes 

But despite everything, both teenagers insist on completing their education. 

Before the war, al-Motouq’s school average was 96 percent. She dreamed of memorising the Quran alongside her twin sister.

'We cried instead of celebrating': War and loss shadow Gaza's top students
Read More »

Today, she has memorised nine of its 30 parts and hopes to continue. 

Junina recently finished high school and is considering studying psychology at university.

People often ask what she wants to become, but she no longer has a clear answer.

“I just want to finish school,” she said, before a brief pause. 

“I want to build a water well as an ongoing charity for my family’s souls.”

Asked what they wished for, both said they just want what children elsewhere take for granted.

“A home, a school, a place where we can live without fear,” al-Motouq said.

“We have the right to learn. We have the right to play. We have the right to have dreams.”

Junina asks for something simpler.

“Treat me like a person,” she said. “Not just as the girl whose family was killed.”

Israel's genocide in Gaza
Gaza City, occupied Palestine

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Iran threatens to block Hormuz if neighbours join US sanctions
item.description:
Iran threatens to block Hormuz if neighbours join US sanctions

Tehran would target the interests of countries that help the United States in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, stated on Saturday.

"We are telling all nearby countries not to join the US economic war, otherwise we will consider them as enemies," Rezaei said, speaking to state television.

He claimed that Trump had been persuaded by Netanyahu to wage an economic war on Iran, saying "The enemy is counting on division and disagreement," while Iran remained "unified."

He directed a particular warning at Gulf states, saying Tehran would retaliate if they join sanctions.

"If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and we will also target other oil export routes from the Persian Gulf."

Iranian security chief also added that Trump's "recklessness" had increased global interest in acquiring nuclear weapons, particularly after it became clear that membership in the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty had failed to prevent US attacks.

"Trump has created nuclear insecurity instead of nuclear security," Rezaei said, adding that his country had accepted international safeguards and complied with IAEA inspections.

"Iran is the only country that is ahead of all other countries in its commitment to nuclear regulations."

"Iran today is not the same Iran as before the war," he said, arguing that perceptions of the US among Iranian youth had shifted, and the image of America as a "peace-loving" nation no longer held.

"The whole world has understood that Trump is a fool."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Hamas says not obligated to implement Trump Gaza deal unless Israel accepts it
item.description:
Hamas says not obligated to implement Trump Gaza deal unless Israel accepts it

Hamas leader Osama Hamdan said the group told US envoy Jared Kushner that it would not consider itself obligated to implement any part of president Trump’s Gaza peace deal unless Israel publicly accepts it and begins implementing its obligations, including halting attacks and withdrawing from Gaza.

Speaking on an Iraqi podcast, Hamdan, a former representative of Hamas in Lebanon and Iran, said the group had not agreed to surrender its weapons. 

He said the framework calls for heavy weapons to be restricted and stored under the authority of a Palestinian administrative committee governing Gaza, while remaining in Palestinian hands.

No weapons would be transferred to any non-Palestinian party, and no fire would be directed outside Gaza under the agreement, he said.

The broader framework includes Israeli withdrawal, lifting the blockade, continued Palestinian governance and security services, and dismantling and disarming collaborator networks.

Hamdan said negotiations over collecting and storing heavy weapons would begin only if Israel accepts the full framework. He said agreeing on the practical mechanism would take time.

“The ball is now in the occupation’s court and with the mediators,” Hamdan said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] GCC, Abu Dhabi-based Muslim Council of Elders condemn Israeli settlement plans
item.description:
GCC, Abu Dhabi-based Muslim Council of Elders condemn Israeli settlement plans

Abu Dhabi-based Muslim Council of Elders and Gulf Cooperation Council have condemned Israeli plans to build a so-called E1 settlement in the occupied West Bank and settlement activities east of occupied Jerusalem.

In a statement carried by Emirates News Agency, the Council said these settlement plans “constitute a flagrant violation of international law and relevant United Nations resolutions”. 

“They also pose a serious threat to efforts aimed at achieving peace in the region and undermine the territorial contiguity of the Occupied Palestinian Territory, particularly between the West Bank and Jerusalem, thereby jeopardizing the prospects for a viable, geographically contiguous, and independent Palestinian state,” the statement read.

Meanwhile, Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), said “advancing these plans represents a blatant challenge to international legitimacy and a systematic undermining of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people”.

"These practices by the Israeli occupation forces undermine the prospects of achieving peace and threaten international and regional efforts aimed at establishing an independent Palestinian state," he said.

Two of the six GCC members—UAE and Bahrain—officially normalised ties with Israel in 2020 under the Abraham Accords.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'Palestinian state already a reality', says Arab Israeli leader Mansour Abbas
item.description:
'Palestinian state already a reality', says Arab Israeli leader Mansour Abbas

Mansour Abbas, the conservative leader of the United Arab List (UAL) party in Israel, has called on Israel to recognise an “independent Palestinian state”, saying that it was already “a reality, which most of the world recognises, with the exception of the United States and Israel”, Israeli media reported.

During a speech to party delegates at their convention in Tayibe on Saturday, Times of Israel reported, Abbas said: “We want them to recognise it, and we’ll work to achieve peace, rapprochement and an end to the occupation and conflict.”

In June 2021, the UAL (Ra'am in its Hebrew acronym) made history by becoming the first independent Arab-majority party to join an Israeli governing coalition.

Abbas’s comments sparked harsh backlash from Israeli prime minister Netanyahu, who said “the price of a left-wing coalition with the Muslim Brotherhood has been exposed once again”, as well as Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot, who said that “there is no Palestinian state”.

item.description:
Macron to host Saudi crown prince for talks on Middle East, energy

French President Emmanuel Macron will be hosting Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman on Sunday for a two-day visit set to range from esports to the war in the Middle East.

Several agreements on health, transport and energy will be signed on the second day of the visit on Monday, according to a French presidential official.

But the visit will kick off in a different style on Sunday evening, with Macron hosting the Saudi leader at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup hosted by Paris.

The event, which brings together the leading performers in esports ranging from computer games to chess and has been eagerly backed by MBS, is being held outside Saudi Arabia for the first time.

On Monday afternoon, MBS and Macron are to chair the first meeting of the Saudi-French strategic partnership council.

Macron and MBS "will discuss key regional issues, in a context calling for close coordination between France and its Gulf partners to foster stability and peace" in the Middle East, according to Macron's office. (Reporting by AFP)

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Aipac told to stay away from pro-Israel Mike Rogers' campaign, report says
item.description:
Aipac told to stay away from pro-Israel Mike Rogers' campaign, report says

Allies of Mike Rogers, a Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, have asked the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) not to run ads on his behalf, according to Axios.

The request came after Rogers spoke with Aipac chair Michael Tuchin in Los Angeles last week. The next day, Aipac shelved an already-prepared video ad targeting Rogers' Democratic rival, Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel.

Axios said the tension underscores how far Aipac’s political standing “has fallen amid voters' anger over the war in Gaza” that even Rogers, a staunchly pro-Israel Republican, “fears the group's public support could be a liability” in the 3 November election.

Aipac had spent more than $30m trying to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and was preparing to spend millions more to help elect Rogers in November, according to people familiar with the talks cited by Axios.

El-Sayed narrowly won his primary against Haley Stevens on 4 August. Axios reports that Rogers' team had warned Aipac beforehand that it expected El-Sayed to win, even as the group held out hope for Stevens.

During the primary, El-Sayed made Aipac 's spending a central target, arguing it showed Stevens was beholden to the pro-Israel lobby. Rogers' campaign believes the strategy backfired by giving El-Sayed a foil he was keen to use again in the general election.

Michigan is home to one of the largest Arab American populations in the US, and a Fox News poll cited by Axios found that 55 percent of Michigan voters oppose continued US aid to Israel.

item.description:
Palestinian commission: Illegal Israeli settlements in West Bank reach 592 by July

The number of illegal Israeli settlements and outposts in the occupied West Bank has reached 592 by the end of July, according to the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission.

The sites comprise 192 settlements and 400 outposts, including 231 pastoral outposts. 

The commission said nearly 780,000 Israeli settlers were living in these settlements: around 333,600 in Jerusalem settlements and 446,400 elsewhere.

Israel now controls over about 42 percent of the West Bank, rising to 71 percent of Area C and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley.

The foreign ministers of Turkey, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE condemned Israel's settlement policies in Palestinian territories and said they categorically rejected the Israeli construction called "E1" in the occupied West Bank.

The new leader of Iran’s top security body has warned its neighbours against joining new US efforts to squeeze Tehran’s economy, and threatened US commercial interests in the region, as Donald Trump doubled down on his fanciful view that the strait of Hormuz was a new US territory.

Those neighbours would be “considered an enemy” and “we will target their interests”, he said.
